lessons.title: Normalization Purpose and Anomalies
lessons.concept: Normalization is the process of organizing relational database tables to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity. It helps prevent anomalies: insertion anomalies (cannot add data without other data), update anomalies (inconsistent updates), and deletion anomalies (unintended loss of data).
lessons.formula: Goal: minimize redundancy, preserve dependencies, avoid anomalies through well-structured relations and keys.
lessons.worked_example: Storing customer address in every order row can cause update anomalies if address changes in some rows but not others. Separating customers into their own table avoids this.
mistakes: Thinking normalization is only about splitting tables randomly
Assuming more tables always mean better performance in every scenario
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: First, Second, and Third Normal Forms (Basics)
lessons.concept: 1NF requires atomic (indivisible) attribute values and no repeating groups. 2NF requires 1NF and that non-key attributes are fully functionally dependent on the whole primary key (relevant for composite keys). 3NF requires 2NF and that non-key attributes are not transitively dependent on the primary key.
lessons.formula: 1NF: atomic values. 2NF: no partial dependency on part of composite key. 3NF: no transitive dependency (non-key -> non-key).
lessons.worked_example: If (OrderID, ProductID) is key and ProductName depends only on ProductID, that partial dependency violates 2NF; move product details to a separate Products table.
mistakes: Applying 2NF concerns when there is no composite key (partial dependency issue doesn't arise)
Confusing transitive dependency with partial dependency
Believing 1NF allows multiple values in a single cell
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Trade-offs and Denormalization Awareness
lessons.concept: Higher normalization improves integrity and reduces redundancy but may require more joins for queries. In some read-heavy scenarios, controlled denormalization is used for performance, with care to manage consistency. Design should balance integrity, complexity, and workload needs.
lessons.formula: Normalized: integrity/reduced redundancy, more joins possible. Denormalized: fewer joins/faster reads sometimes, higher redundancy/update risk.
lessons.worked_example: A reporting table may store precomputed aggregates (denormalized) for speed, while source-of-truth tables remain normalized.

practice.question: Normalization primarily aims to:

options.B: Reduce redundancy and improve data integrity

practice.explanation: Normalization organizes tables to minimize redundancy and prevent data anomalies, improving integrity.

practice.question: A table is in 1NF when:

options.B: All attributes contain atomic (indivisible) values and no repeating groups

practice.explanation: First Normal Form requires that each field holds atomic values and there are no repeating groups/arrays in a single attribute.

practice.question: Partial dependency (relevant to 2NF) occurs when:

options.A: A non-key attribute depends on part of a composite primary key
options.C: A key depends on a non-key attribute
options.D: All attributes depend on the full key

practice.explanation: 2NF removes partial dependencies, where a non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite key rather than the whole key.
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

practice.question: Transitive dependency (addressed in 3NF) means:

options.A: A non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute
options.B: A table depends on another database
options.C: The primary key has multiple columns

practice.explanation: In 3NF, non-key attributes must depend only on the key; a non-key depending on another non-key indicates transitive dependency.

practice.question: An update anomaly is:

options.B: Inconsistent data due to the same fact updated in some places but not others

practice.explanation: Redundant storage of the same information can lead to inconsistencies when updates are applied partially, causing update anomalies.

questions.question: Which anomaly occurs when deleting a row also removes unintended important information?
questions.explanation: A deletion anomaly happens when removing one piece of data inadvertently deletes other necessary data due to poor table design.
